growth.juvenile_note: Seed germinates within a day or two on fresh, wet river gravel and silt after the spring floods. Seedlings and saplings form dense thickets of slender single stems with glossy, diamond- to triangular-ovate, finely toothed leaves on flattened stalks that tremble; young shoots are often reddish. Broken branches and toppled trunks root readily, so many young trees are clones.
growth.source: JRC European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (to 40 m and 200 cm dbh; mature trees live 100, occasionally 300-400 yr; light-demanding pioneer, fast growing, wind pollinated, flowers before the leaves); Wikipedia (20-30 m, rarely 40 m). Germination and age at first flowering estimated from Populus.

fruiting.source: JRC Atlas (flowers before leaves; wind pollinated; fluffy seeds from capsules in catkins, spread by wind and water). Colour is the crimson male catkins. Catkin and capsule sizes, ripening (seed shed May-June) and crop estimated from Populus deltoides and other poplars.

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal germination: the nut stays in the soil and a deep taproot races down before the shoot grows much. The seedling is a slim single whip with pinnate leaves; the first leaves have few (3-7) leaflets, later ones 9-17 sickle-shaped leaflets. It keeps a straight leader and narrow crown for years before spreading into a broad dome.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Carya illinoinensis (flowers Mar-May; nuts mature Sep-Oct, seedfall to Dec; seed production from ~20 yr, peak 75-225 yr; ~100 lb nuts/yr; seedlings to 3 ft/yr; shade intolerant; 30-45 m); USDA Silvics (lives and bears >300 yr)

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS/Silvics (male catkins in threes, pistillate spikes of few flowers at shoot tips, wind-pollinated, Mar-May; nut in a four-winged husk that splits, mature Sep-Oct, fall through Dec; ~100 lb/yr from mature trees); nut counts per lb from pecan extension guides

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two narrow cotyledons, then broad, maple-like, shallowly lobed leaves; it needs bare, sunlit, moist soil such as river sandbars. Saplings are fast, slender whips with zigzag twigs and big leaves; smooth bark soon flakes into a camouflage patchwork, creamy white on the upper limbs.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Wells & Schmidtling): open-grown trees seed at 6-7 yrs, peak at 50-200; seed germinates far better in light; a 17-year NC plantation averaged over 21 m; intermediate shade tolerance; can exceed 250 years, largest to 51 m tall

growth.juvenile_note: Germinates within a day on wet silt: a tiny seedling with 2 round cotyledons. The young tree is a fast, slender whip (often 1-2 m a year) with narrow lance leaves silvery-silky beneath and upward-angled branches; later a broad, irregular, often leaning crown over water. Broken twigs root easily; pollarding gives the classic knobbly 'pollard willow'.
growth.source: EUFORGEN Salix alba (20-30 m, fast-growing, short-lived, seed viable only briefly); PFAF (to 25 m at a fast rate; flowers Apr-May, seed ripe in June; seed viable only a few days); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix (willow seed has no dormancy and germinates within 12-24 h on wet ground (USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix)); growth curve and age at first seed estimated from Salix nigra

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two large, round, fleshy pale-green cotyledons on a translucent, succulent, pink-tinged stem, often in dense carpets in early spring after winter chilling. Leaves are soft, oval, bluntly toothed and water-repellent (silvery when wet). Plants shoot up to waist height within a few months and branch, hanging orange spurred flowers and explosive pods from mid-summer to frost.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Impatiens capensis: annual 0.9-1.5 m, blooms late spring to early fall, cleistogamous flowers, explosive capsules); spring germination after winter chilling is typical of the species; germination days and growth fractions estimated from that phenology.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two small round cotyledons, then pairs of opposite, oval, coarsely toothed leaves that already carry stinging hairs. The seedling is one upright four-angled stem at first; during its first season it sends yellow rhizomes and stolons outward, so a year-old plant is a small patch of unbranched square stems that die back to the ground each winter and re-emerge in spring.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Urtica dioica): non-dormant seed germinates 5-10 days after maturity; stems 1-2 m; a rhizome planted in late summer spreads 2.5 m across by the next year; probably intermediate in shade tolerance, more seed in sun (10,000-20,000 per shoot); flowers late May-Oct. Wikipedia: 0.9-2 m, dies down in winter. First flowering and clump life estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two oval, short-stalked cotyledons, then alternate, heart-shaped, coarsely toothed leaves on a thin green stem. In its first year the seedling is a short floppy shoot; forked tendrils opposite the leaves appear within a few nodes and it becomes a scrambling vine that sprawls over the ground or brush until it finds a stem to climb, then runs several metres a year toward light.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Vitis riparia): long-lived climbing vine with trunks several inches thick, hardy to -57 C; USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Vitis): riverbank grape seed needs about 90 days of cold stratification. Germination after stratification, growth, first fruiting and ages estimated from wild grapes.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (Vitis riparia): small fragrant white or greenish flowers Apr-Jun in loose panicles 4-15 cm, functionally dioecious; blue-black, sour, herbaceous, juicy berries 6-15 mm ripe in Aug-Sep, used for jelly, jam and wine. Pollinator mix, fruit set, persistence into winter and crop estimated.
